A written quote is a small piece of paper. But it tells you almost everything you need to know about the company handing it to you.

If a contractor is willing to put a number in writing, itemized, before they touch your property, it usually means they know exactly what the job requires and they are confident enough in that number to stand behind it. If a contractor avoids giving you anything in writing, or gives you a vague verbal range instead, that should tell you something too.

At Max Haas Septic, every new septic install starts with a written quote. Here is exactly what that means, what goes into it, and what happens after you sign it.

WHY WE DO NOT QUOTE OVER THE PHONE

We understand the instinct to want a number quickly. You are trying to plan a budget, maybe comparing us against other companies, and a fast answer feels helpful.

But a phone quote for a septic install is really just a guess. Your soil, your water table, your lot's accessibility, and your household size all affect what system your property needs and what it costs. None of that can be determined without someone actually walking your property.

So instead of guessing, we send a technician to your property first. That visit is what our written quote is based on, which is exactly why you can trust the number once you have it.

WHAT HAPPENS DURING YOUR SITE EVALUATION

A technician walks your lot and evaluates your soil conditions, drainage, and where a tank and drain field could realistically go given your property lines and any well or water source you have. We discuss your household size and expected water usage, since that determines system sizing. We talk through your timeline and any specific concerns you have about your property.

This visit typically takes less time than people expect, and at the end of it, you are not left wondering what happens next. We tell you what we saw, what we recommend, and roughly what to expect before the formal written quote follows.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN YOUR WRITTEN QUOTE

This is the part most companies do not explain, so here it is in plain terms. Your written quote includes:

The system type recommended for your property, and a plain-language explanation of why that system fits your soil and household size, rather than a different, possibly less expensive option that would not hold up.

An itemized breakdown of materials and labor, so you can see what you are paying for, not just a single lump number.

The estimated cost of permitting through your county health department, which varies depending on which of the nine counties we serve your property is in.

A realistic timeline, from permit approval to the day the system is installed and inspected.

What is NOT included, so there is no ambiguity, such as unrelated landscaping repair beyond standard grading and backfill, or work outside the agreed system design.

You can read every line, ask questions about anything unclear, and decide whether to move forward, all before a single shovel goes into the ground.

WHAT HAPPENS IF SOMETHING UNEXPECTED COMES UP

Underground work occasionally turns up something that could not have been identified during the site evaluation; an unmarked utility line, unusual rock, or subsurface conditions that were not visible from the surface. This is uncommon, but if it happens, we stop and talk to you about it directly before doing any additional work or adjusting the cost. You are never presented with a surprise line item on a final invoice for work you never approved.

THE WARRANTY AND SUPPORT THAT COMES AFTER INSTALLATION

The written quote covers the cost of the job. What happens after installation is just as important, and it is part of why homeowners across Central Indiana trust us with a system that has to function correctly for decades.

Once your system is installed and passes final inspection, we stand behind the work. If something related to our installation needs attention, you are calling the company that designed and built your system and already knows every detail about your property, not starting over with someone unfamiliar with what is in your yard.

We can also walk you through the basic maintenance your specific system will need going forward, including a realistic pumping schedule, so you are not guessing five or ten years from now about whether something needs attention. If you ever have a question about your system, whether it is two months or ten years after installation, you are calling a team that has your property's actual records on file, not explaining your situation from scratch to someone new.

A FEW QUESTIONS WE GET ABOUT THE QUOTE PROCESS

"Does the site evaluation cost anything?"

No. The evaluation is free, and it is how we generate an accurate written quote. There is no obligation to move forward with the install just because you had a technician look at your property.

"How long is the written quote good for?"

We will tell you the specific window when you receive it, but in general, pricing on materials and labor is not something we intend to change on you shortly after handing you a number. If a significant amount of time passes before you are ready to move forward, we may need to revisit the quote, and we will tell you plainly if that is the case.

"What if I get a quote and decide not to move forward?"

That is entirely your decision. A written quote is information, not a contract you are locked into by requesting it. Some homeowners request quotes to plan a future budget, others because they are actively comparing companies. Either reason is fine.

"Can I ask questions about the quote before deciding?"

Yes, and we would rather you did. If a line item is unclear, or you want to understand why we recommended a particular system type over a less expensive option, ask. A quote you do not fully understand is not actually useful to you, regardless of how accurate the number is.

"What makes your quote different from a rough estimate somewhere else?"

The difference is what the number is based on. A rough estimate given without a site visit is based on averages and assumptions. Our written quote is based on an actual technician standing on your actual property, looking at your actual soil and layout. That is the entire reason it holds up once the work begins, instead of changing halfway through the job.

WHAT A WRITTEN QUOTE PROTECTS YOU FROM

Homeowners who skip this step, who hire based on a verbal number over the phone, are the ones most likely to end up with a final bill that does not match what they expected. Not necessarily because the contractor was dishonest, but because nobody actually confirmed what the property needed before work started. Assumptions made without a site visit have a way of becoming expensive corrections once the ground is already open.

A written quote, built from a real site evaluation, removes that risk before it exists. You know the system type, the itemized cost, the timeline, and what is and is not included, before you agree to anything. There is no version of this process where you are surprised by the final invoice, because the final invoice matches the written quote you already reviewed and approved.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE FOR A SEPTIC SYSTEM THAN ALMOST ANY OTHER HOME PROJECT

Most home improvement projects are visible. You can look at a new roof or a repainted room and judge the quality yourself. A septic system is buried. Once it is backfilled, you cannot see the workmanship anymore, which means you are trusting the installer's judgment on something you will never personally inspect again unless it fails.

That is exactly why a written quote, a documented process, and a company willing to stand behind the finished work matter so much here. You are not just buying a system. You are buying the judgment and accountability of the people who buried it.

WHERE WE WORK

We provide written quotes and complete septic installs across Marion, Hamilton, Hendricks, Boone, Johnson, Morgan, Hancock, Shelby, and Madison counties in Central Indiana.

HOW TO GET YOUR WRITTEN QUOTE

Request your free quote below. You will answer a few short questions about your property and your timeline, and someone from Max Haas Septic will follow up to schedule your site evaluation. From there, you get a real, itemized number in writing, based on an actual look at your property, not a guess over the phone.

No pressure to sign on the spot. No vague verbal estimate you have to try to remember later. Just a clear, written quote you can actually trust, from a team that stands behind it after the work is done.

Get your free quote today.

P.S. If another company has already given you a verbal number without ever visiting your property, ask them to put it in writing before you agree to anything. If they hesitate, that tells you something important before you hire them, not after.

When did your septic tank last get pumped? If you had to think about it, read this.

Most people in Georgia on septic can't say when their tank was last serviced. Previous owners don't leave records, and nothing in the house reminds you. The system just works quietly until it doesn't.

A septic system is a tank plus a drainfield. The tank holds solids so the drainfield only receives liquid. When the tank is neglected, solids reach the drainfield, and a clogged drainfield often means a repair far larger than a pump-out.

The common mistake is treating the tank as "fine because nothing's wrong." Slow drains, soggy ground, and odors are late signs, not early ones.

Here's how we handle it. We come out, pump the tank, and check the system while it's open. You get a straight answer on its condition and a recommended pumping schedule based on your tank size and household. If a repair is ever needed, we explain what and why before anything starts.

If you bought a home on septic in the Atlanta area, there's a good chance you don't know what shape your tank is in.

You're not alone.

Most homeowners don't. Here's why that matters, and a simple way to fix it.

THE HOME YOU BOUGHT HAS A HIDDEN SYSTEM

When you buy a house on city sewer, the system is the city's problem.

When you buy a house on septic, it's yours.

The tank, the lines, the drainfield. All of it sits in your yard, and all of it is your responsibility.

Yet most people move in with almost no information.

The seller may have mentioned a pump-out. Maybe there's an old receipt in a drawer. Maybe not.

So the system runs quietly in the background, and you assume it's fine.

Often it is.

But "probably fine" isn't a plan.

WHAT YOU DON'T KNOW CAN'T BE FIXED EARLY

Septic problems tend to be gradual.

A baffle cracks. A filter slowly clogs. Sludge builds up a little more each month.

None of it announces itself.

There's no warning light. No monthly bill that jumps. The first sign most people see is a slow drain, a soggy spot, or a backup.

By then, the problem has had months or years to develop.

Catching it earlier, when it's a small repair or just a pump-out, is almost always easier and cheaper.

WHAT A MAINTENANCE VISIT LOOKS AT

A good maintenance visit has a simple goal: to find out where your system stands.

Here is what that involves.

The tank is located and opened. Lids and access points are checked.

The tank is pumped, so the inside can actually be seen.

The condition of the tank and its working parts is looked over. That includes the inlet and outlet, and any filter that's installed.

The way the tank refills and holds its level is noted, because that can reveal trouble beyond the tank.

Then you get a straight answer: what looks healthy, what doesn't, and when to schedule the next visit.

THE COMMON MISTAKES NEW OWNERS MAKE

MISTAKE 1: Assuming the inspection at closing covered everything.

A home inspection may confirm that a septic system exists and appears to be working that day. That is not the same as knowing what's inside the tank, or when it was last pumped.

MISTAKE 2: Not knowing where the tank is.

If you can't find your tank, you can't service it. Many homeowners have never seen their lids.

MISTAKE 3: Guessing at a schedule.

"Every five years" is a rule of thumb. Your tank size and household decide the right number.

MISTAKE 4: Waiting for a problem to prove you right.

A system that seems fine today may be overdue. Waiting for proof usually means paying for it.

A SHORT TOUR OF YOUR SYSTEM

Here's a plain-English tour of what's in your yard.

Pipe from the house. Everything you flush or drain leaves through one main line and heads toward the tank.

The tank. Usually concrete, fiberglass, or plastic, buried a short distance from the house. Its job is to hold waste long enough for solids and liquids to separate.

The outlet. Liquid leaves the tank through an outlet pipe, sometimes through a filter.

The drainfield. A series of trenches or pipes that spread the liquid into the soil, where it's naturally treated.

Some homes also have a pump system, which moves liquid uphill or across a long distance. Others have alternative systems, like drip or aerobic systems, which have more parts and need their own care.

Knowing which type you have is the first step to caring for it properly.

HOW TO FIND YOUR TANK

If you've never located your tank, here are a few places to start.

Check your closing documents or any paperwork from the previous owner. A system diagram sometimes comes with them.

Look at the yard. Tanks are usually in the area where the main sewer line leaves the house.

Look for a slight mound, a patch of grass that grows differently, or a round or rectangular lid at ground level.

Don't dig randomly and don't probe near the drainfield.

Or skip all that and tell us when we call. We'll help you work it out.

SIGNS YOUR SYSTEM NEEDS ATTENTION

Maintenance should happen before any of these. But if you've noticed one, it's worth a call.

Drains that run slowly throughout the house.

Gurgling sounds from pipes or toilets.

Sewage odors indoors or near the tank.

Wet, spongy ground, or unusually green grass over the tank or drainfield.

Water backing up in tubs or toilets.

Any one of these can have several causes. The only way to know is to have the system looked at.

IF YOU'RE THINKING OF SELLING

Septic is one of the things a buyer's inspector will ask about.

A recent pump-out, with a record of what was found, takes a question mark out of the sale.

It also gives you time to deal with anything small before it becomes a negotiating issue.

If you plan to list in the next year or two, doing the maintenance now is cheaper than doing it under a deadline.

WHY WE SAY "KNOW YOUR TANK"

There's a simple idea behind how we approach maintenance.

You shouldn't have to guess.

Septic is one of the few things in a home that's completely out of sight. That makes a good explanation more valuable than usual.

When our technician finishes at your home, you should be able to answer three questions.

What condition is my system in?

Is anything likely to need attention soon?

When should I schedule the next visit?

If you can answer those, you can plan.

And if you can plan, a septic system is just another part of the house.

WHAT YOU'LL GET FROM A ONE WAY VISIT

You'll get a clear call from us when you ask for service, and we'll explain what the visit includes.

You'll get a technician who opens the tank, pumps it, and checks the system while it's open.

You'll get a plain explanation of what he sees, with no jargon.

You'll get a recommended pumping schedule that fits your home.

And if something needs repair, you'll hear what it is and why, before anything extra happens.

You decide what comes next.

FIVE THINGS THAT QUIETLY HURT A SEPTIC SYSTEM

You don't need to be perfect. But these are worth avoiding.

Pouring grease or cooking oil down the drain.

Flushing wipes, even ones labeled flushable.

Running a garbage disposal heavily.

Driving or parking over the tank or drainfield.

Pouring strong chemicals or large amounts of bleach down the drain.

Each one makes the tank fill faster, or disturbs the balance of what's happening inside.

Septic systems usually give warnings before they fail.

Drains that run slowly, in more than one spot in the house.

Gurgling sounds from pipes when water runs.

A sewage smell indoors or around the yard.

Wet, spongy ground near the tank or drainfield.

A patch of grass that is greener and lusher than the rest of the lawn.

Any one of these is worth a call. Catching it early usually means a simpler fix.

quote","cards":[],"body":{"text":"A written quote is a small piece of paper. But it tells you almost everything you need to know about the company handing it to you.

If a contractor is willing to put a number in writing, itemized, before they touch your property, it usually means they know exactly what the job requires and they are confident enough in that number to stand behind it. If a contractor avoids giving you anything in writing, or gives you a vague verbal range instead, that should tell you something too.

At Max Haas Septic, every new septic install starts with a written quote. Here is exactly what that means, what goes into it, and what happens after you sign it.

WHY WE DO NOT QUOTE OVER THE PHONE

We understand the instinct to want a number quickly. You are trying to plan a budget, maybe comparing us against other companies, and a fast answer feels helpful.

But a phone quote for a septic install is really just a guess. Your soil, your water table, your lot's accessibility, and your household size all affect what system your property needs and what it costs. None of that can be determined without someone actually walking your property.

So instead of guessing, we send a technician to your property first. That visit is what our written quote is based on, which is exactly why you can trust the number once you have it.

WHAT HAPPENS DURING YOUR SITE EVALUATION

A technician walks your lot and evaluates your soil conditions, drainage, and where a tank and drain field could realistically go given your property lines and any well or water source you have. We discuss your household size and expected water usage, since that determines system sizing. We talk through your timeline and any specific concerns you have about your property.

This visit typically takes less time than people expect, and at the end of it, you are not left wondering what happens next. We tell you what we saw, what we recommend, and roughly what to expect before the formal written quote follows.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN YOUR WRITTEN QUOTE

This is the part most companies do not explain, so here it is in plain terms. Your written quote includes:

The system type recommended for your property, and a plain-language explanation of why that system fits your soil and household size, rather than a different, possibly less expensive option that would not hold up.

An itemized breakdown of materials and labor, so you can see what you are paying for, not just a single lump number.

The estimated cost of permitting through your county health department, which varies depending on which of the nine counties we serve your property is in.

A realistic timeline, from permit approval to the day the system is installed and inspected.

What is NOT included, so there is no ambiguity, such as unrelated landscaping repair beyond standard grading and backfill, or work outside the agreed system design.

You can read every line, ask questions about anything unclear, and decide whether to move forward, all before a single shovel goes into the ground.

WHAT HAPPENS IF SOMETHING UNEXPECTED COMES UP

Underground work occasionally turns up something that could not have been identified during the site evaluation; an unmarked utility line, unusual rock, or subsurface conditions that were not visible from the surface. This is uncommon, but if it happens, we stop and talk to you about it directly before doing any additional work or adjusting the cost. You are never presented with a surprise line item on a final invoice for work you never approved.

THE WARRANTY AND SUPPORT THAT COMES AFTER INSTALLATION

The written quote covers the cost of the job. What happens after installation is just as important, and it is part of why homeowners across Central Indiana trust us with a system that has to function correctly for decades.

Once your system is installed and passes final inspection, we stand behind the work. If something related to our installation needs attention, you are calling the company that designed and built your system and already knows every detail about your property, not starting over with someone unfamiliar with what is in your yard.

We can also walk you through the basic maintenance your specific system will need going forward, including a realistic pumping schedule, so you are not guessing five or ten years from now about whether something needs attention. If you ever have a question about your system, whether it is two months or ten years after installation, you are calling a team that has your property's actual records on file, not explaining your situation from scratch to someone new.

A FEW QUESTIONS WE GET ABOUT THE QUOTE PROCESS

"Does the site evaluation cost anything?"

No. The evaluation is free, and it is how we generate an accurate written quote. There is no obligation to move forward with the install just because you had a technician look at your property.

"How long is the written quote good for?"

We will tell you the specific window when you receive it, but in general, pricing on materials and labor is not something we intend to change on you shortly after handing you a number. If a significant amount of time passes before you are ready to move forward, we may need to revisit the quote, and we will tell you plainly if that is the case.

"What if I get a quote and decide not to move forward?"

That is entirely your decision. A written quote is information, not a contract you are locked into by requesting it. Some homeowners request quotes to plan a future budget, others because they are actively comparing companies. Either reason is fine.

"Can I ask questions about the quote before deciding?"

Yes, and we would rather you did. If a line item is unclear, or you want to understand why we recommended a particular system type over a less expensive option, ask. A quote you do not fully understand is not actually useful to you, regardless of how accurate the number is.

"What makes your quote different from a rough estimate somewhere else?"

The difference is what the number is based on. A rough estimate given without a site visit is based on averages and assumptions. Our written quote is based on an actual technician standing on your actual property, looking at your actual soil and layout. That is the entire reason it holds up once the work begins, instead of changing halfway through the job.

WHAT A WRITTEN QUOTE PROTECTS YOU FROM

Homeowners who skip this step, who hire based on a verbal number over the phone, are the ones most likely to end up with a final bill that does not match what they expected. Not necessarily because the contractor was dishonest, but because nobody actually confirmed what the property needed before work started. Assumptions made without a site visit have a way of becoming expensive corrections once the ground is already open.

A written quote, built from a real site evaluation, removes that risk before it exists. You know the system type, the itemized cost, the timeline, and what is and is not included, before you agree to anything. There is no version of this process where you are surprised by the final invoice, because the final invoice matches the written quote you already reviewed and approved.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE FOR A SEPTIC SYSTEM THAN ALMOST ANY OTHER HOME PROJECT

Most home improvement projects are visible. You can look at a new roof or a repainted room and judge the quality yourself. A septic system is buried. Once it is backfilled, you cannot see the workmanship anymore, which means you are trusting the installer's judgment on something you will never personally inspect again unless it fails.

That is exactly why a written quote, a documented process, and a company willing to stand behind the finished work matter so much here. You are not just buying a system. You are buying the judgment and accountability of the people who buried it.

WHERE WE WORK

We provide written quotes and complete septic installs across Marion, Hamilton, Hendricks, Boone, Johnson, Morgan, Hancock, Shelby, and Madison counties in Central Indiana.

HOW TO GET YOUR WRITTEN QUOTE

Request your free quote below. You will answer a few short questions about your property and your timeline, and someone from Max Haas Septic will follow up to schedule your site evaluation. From there, you get a real, itemized number in writing, based on an actual look at your property, not a guess over the phone.

No pressure to sign on the spot. No vague verbal estimate you have to try to remember later. Just a clear, written quote you can actually trust, from a team that stands behind it after the work is done.

Get your free quote today.

P.S. If another company has already given you a verbal number without ever visiting your property, ask them to put it in writing before you agree to anything. A septic system is a tank plus a drainfield. The tank holds solids so the drainfield only receives liquid. When the tank is neglected, solids reach the drainfield, and a clogged drainfield often means a repair far larger than a pump-out.

The common mistake is treating the tank as "fine because nothing's wrong." Slow drains, soggy ground, and odors are late signs, not early ones.

more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"If you bought a home on septic in the Atlanta area, there's a good chance you don't know what shape your tank is in.

You're not alone.

Most homeowners don't. Here's why that matters, and a simple way to fix it.

THE HOME YOU BOUGHT HAS A HIDDEN SYSTEM

When you buy a house on city sewer, the system is the city's problem.

When you buy a house on septic, it's yours.

The tank, the lines, the drainfield. All of it sits in your yard, and all of it is your responsibility.

Yet most people move in with almost no information.

The seller may have mentioned a pump-out. Maybe there's an old receipt in a drawer. Maybe not.

So the system runs quietly in the background, and you assume it's fine.

Often it is.

But "probably fine" isn't a plan.

WHAT YOU DON'T KNOW CAN'T BE FIXED EARLY

Septic problems tend to be gradual.

A baffle cracks. A filter slowly clogs. Sludge builds up a little more each month.

None of it announces itself.

There's no warning light. No monthly bill that jumps. The first sign most people see is a slow drain, a soggy spot, or a backup.

By then, the problem has had months or years to develop.

Catching it earlier, when it's a small repair or just a pump-out, is almost always easier and cheaper.

WHAT A MAINTENANCE VISIT LOOKS AT

A good maintenance visit has a simple goal: to find out where your system stands.

Here is what that involves.

The tank is located and opened. Lids and access points are checked.

The tank is pumped, so the inside can actually be seen.

The condition of the tank and its working parts is looked over. That includes the inlet and outlet, and any filter that's installed.

The way the tank refills and holds its level is noted, because that can reveal trouble beyond the tank.

Then you get a straight answer: what looks healthy, what doesn't, and when to schedule the next visit.

THE COMMON MISTAKES NEW OWNERS MAKE

MISTAKE 1: Assuming the inspection at closing covered everything.

A home inspection may confirm that a septic system exists and appears to be working that day. That is not the same as knowing what's inside the tank, or when it was last pumped.

MISTAKE 2: Not knowing where the tank is.

If you can't find your tank, you can't service it. Many homeowners have never seen their lids.

MISTAKE 3: Guessing at a schedule.

"Every five years" is a rule of thumb. Your tank size and household decide the right number.

MISTAKE 4: Waiting for a problem to prove you right.

A system that seems fine today may be overdue. Waiting for proof usually means paying for it.

A SHORT TOUR OF YOUR SYSTEM

Here's a plain-English tour of what's in your yard.

Pipe from the house. Everything you flush or drain leaves through one main line and heads toward the tank.

The tank. Usually concrete, fiberglass, or plastic, buried a short distance from the house. Its job is to hold waste long enough for solids and liquids to separate.

The outlet. Liquid leaves the tank through an outlet pipe, sometimes through a filter.

The drainfield. A series of trenches or pipes that spread the liquid into the soil, where it's naturally treated.

Some homes also have a pump system, which moves liquid uphill or across a long distance. Others have alternative systems, like drip or aerobic systems, which have more parts and need their own care.

Knowing which type you have is the first step to caring for it properly.

HOW TO FIND YOUR TANK

If you've never located your tank, here are a few places to start.

Check your closing documents or any paperwork from the previous owner. A system diagram sometimes comes with them.

Look at the yard. Tanks are usually in the area where the main sewer line leaves the house.

Look for a slight mound, a patch of grass that grows differently, or a round or rectangular lid at ground level.

Don't dig randomly and don't probe near the drainfield.

Or skip all that and tell us when we call. We'll help you work it out.

SIGNS YOUR SYSTEM NEEDS ATTENTION

Maintenance should happen before any of these. But if you've noticed one, it's worth a call.

Drains that run slowly throughout the house.

Gurgling sounds from pipes or toilets.

Sewage odors indoors or near the tank.

Wet, spongy ground, or unusually green grass over the tank or drainfield.

Water backing up in tubs or toilets.

Any one of these can have several causes. The only way to know is to have the system looked at.

IF YOU'RE THINKING OF SELLING

Septic is one of the things a buyer's inspector will ask about.

A recent pump-out, with a record of what was found, takes a question mark out of the sale.

It also gives you time to deal with anything small before it becomes a negotiating issue.

If you plan to list in the next year or two, doing the maintenance now is cheaper than doing it under a deadline.

WHY WE SAY "KNOW YOUR TANK"

There's a simple idea behind how we approach maintenance.

You shouldn't have to guess.

Septic is one of the few things in a home that's completely out of sight. That makes a good explanation more valuable than usual.

When our technician finishes at your home, you should be able to answer three questions.

What condition is my system in?

Is anything likely to need attention soon?

When should I schedule the next visit?

If you can answer those, you can plan.

And if you can plan, a septic system is just another part of the house.

WHAT YOU'LL GET FROM A ONE WAY VISIT

You'll get a clear call from us when you ask for service, and we'll explain what the visit includes.

You'll get a technician who opens the tank, pumps it, and checks the system while it's open.

You'll get a plain explanation of what he sees, with no jargon.

You'll get a recommended pumping schedule that fits your home.

And if something needs repair, you'll hear what it is and why, before anything extra happens.

You decide what comes next.

FIVE THINGS THAT QUIETLY HURT A SEPTIC SYSTEM

You don't need to be perfect. But these are worth avoiding.

Pouring grease or cooking oil down the drain.

Flushing wipes, even ones labeled flushable.

Running a garbage disposal heavily.

Driving or parking over the tank or drainfield.

Pouring strong chemicals or large amounts of bleach down the drain.

Each one makes the tank fill faster, or disturbs the balance of what's happening inside.

SIGNS YOUR TANK NEEDS ATTENTION

Septic systems usually give warnings before they fail.

Drains that run slowly, in more than one spot in the house.

Gurgling sounds from pipes when water runs.

A sewage smell indoors or around the yard.

Wet, spongy ground near the tank or drainfield.

A patch of grass that is greener and lusher than the rest of the lawn.

Any one of these is worth a call. Catching it early usually means a simpler fix.

A NOTE ON REPAIRS

Most maintenance visits end with a pump-out and a schedule.

Sometimes a visit turns up a repair need.

When it does, we can handle it. We service drainfields, outlet pipes, sewer and main lines, alternative systems, and pump systems.

But that's never the starting point.

The starting point is finding out what's real. Then we talk about options.

WHO WE ARE

One Way Septic & Sewer is a family-owned company in Acworth, Georgia.

Jody Harrison's family has been in septic since 1953, and Jody started One Way in 2018. We focus on residential septic service, which means homeowners, not developers.

We serve Bartow, Carroll, Cherokee, Cobb, DeKalb, Douglas, Forsyth, Fulton and Paulding counties.

HOW TO GET STARTED

Tap Learn More, answer a few quick questions, and we'll call you to schedule. No obligation.

On that call we'll ask when your tank was last pumped, how many people live in the home, and whether you've noticed anything unusual.

QUICK QUESTIONS

I just moved in. Should I schedule a pump-out right away?

If you don't know when the tank was last pumped, it's a good idea. It gives you a clean starting point and a written schedule.

I haven't noticed any problems. Is a visit still worth it?

Yes. Maintenance is meant to happen before problems appear.

What if I can't find my tank?

Tell us. Locating it is part of what we can help with.

What if you find something wrong?

We'll explain what you're seeing and what the options are. You decide.

How long does a visit take?

We'll give you a realistic idea when we call, once we know your tank size and access.

What do I need to have ready?

Just clear access to the tank area. We'll walk you through it on the phone.

THE SIMPLE VERSION

Your septic system is out of sight, so it's easy to forget.

A maintenance visit turns it from a mystery into something you understand.

Tap Learn More and tell us about your home.

We'll call you and set up a time.

P.S. If you're new to your home, or you can't remember your last pump-out, this is a simple way to start with real information about your system. Hi, I'm Sarah, and I'm a board-certified lactation consultant, an IBCLC, who has spent the last eleven years working with nothing but new mothers who were told their supply was too low.

I've sat with THOUSANDS of these moms, and they all tell me the same story. They pumped around the clock for six weeks and got nothing but drops and cracked nipples. They spent a fortune on lactation cookies and teas and drank so much water they felt sick. They tried fenugreek and it made the baby gassy and, for a lot of them, made their supply worse, not better. They bought the bargain-bin supplements with a long list of herbs on the label and a sprinkle of each one inside, too little of anything to do a thing. They power pumped at 2 a.m. until they had nothing left. And they were still losing.

And when they finally went back to their provider, exhausted and in tears, they got the same answer almost every time. "Be patient, it takes time. Some women just can't. Your supply is probably just low. Let's top up with a little formula and see."

But here's what nobody tells you. It is almost never that your body can't make the milk. It's what happens to one specific reflex when you're running on no sleep, in pain, and terrified. Let me explain.

There are two hormones running this whole system, and they do two completely different jobs. Prolactin makes the milk. It fills thousands of tiny sacs deep in the breast. For most moms, that part is working fine, that's the full, heavy, aching feeling, a breast full of milk. The second hormone, oxytocin, is the one that releases it. It squeezes those sacs so the milk comes down and out. That's the letdown. And oxytocin is shy. It only surges when you feel calm and safe. The moment you're stressed, exhausted, or afraid, your body floods with cortisol, and cortisol shuts that oxytocin surge down. So the milk gets made, and it just sits there, locked in.

Now here's where it gets important. The pump, the thing everyone hands you and tells you to use more, does not create the letdown. It can only pull milk that has already let down. It needs that oxytocin surge to fire first. Without it, after the first few minutes there's nothing left to release, and the pump is just tugging on tissue, giving you drops. Same with the cookies, the oats, the gallons of water, and the sprinkle-dose herb capsules, they're all trying to force more milk into a breast that's already full, while not one of them touches the reflex that's actually stuck, and not one of them is dosed high enough to move a hormone anyway.

And here's the part that shows how broken this is. A huge share of the moms told they have "low supply" were never once checked for a blocked letdown. They were handed a pump and a can of formula and sent home to "be patient," when the milk was there the whole time and the reflex to release it was jammed. Nobody told them. Not the appointment, not the commercials, not the subscription boxes. Nobody.

So when your breasts feel full but the pump gives you drops, when you scoop hair-thin streams into a bottle at 3 a.m. and count the ounces, when your baby pulls off a full breast and screams, when you hand him to someone else to calm him because you can't, You think it's YOUR failure. You think your body is broken. You think you waited too long, or you're just not one of the women who can.

But that's not what happened. What happened is you were handed a tool that can only empty a breast that has already let down, and a reflex that was locked shut by stress, and then you were told to be patient while it got worse.

I watched this happen in my own practice for years. Moms drowning, quitting, blaming themselves, and I kept saying "pump more, stay hydrated, be patient," because that's what we're trained to say. And I was part of the problem. I was sending women home to fight a locked door with a tool that couldn't open it.

But here's the thing. There's a way to support both jobs at once, the making AND the releasing, without forcing output and without a prescription. It's not a drug. It's a set of plants mothers have leaned on for generations, but with one catch almost every product on the shelf gets wrong. Let me walk you through it.

The core is a plant matrix, moringa, fennel, milk thistle, and blessed thistle. These are traditional galactagogues, and the point is that they work on the hormones, not on calories. Some of them support the prolactin side, so there's plenty of milk in the sacs. And, just as important, the blend helps ease the stress load that's jamming oxytocin, so the letdown can finally fire and the milk that's already there can come down. Both sides. The making and the releasing. But here's the catch nobody talks about, and it's the whole reason those bargain supplements do nothing. These plants only move the hormones at a real, concentrated dose. Most products list all the right herbs and then put a tiny pinch of each one in, just enough to print on the label, not remotely enough to do anything in your body. It's like trying to season a whole pot of soup with a single grain of salt. Get the same plants at the correct, concentrated dose, and the exact same botanicals that "didn't work" for years suddenly do.

And here's what makes it more than a milk booster. On top of the concentrated plant matrix, it carries DHA and choline, which support your baby's brain and make richer, fattier milk. Vitamin D3, because breast milk is often low in it. And B12, for the bone-deep postpartum fatigue you've probably been calling your new personality. So you're not just working on supply, you're refueling the mom the whole system runs on. No fenugreek, which crashes supply for a lot of women. No prescription. No side effects to white-knuckle through. Just the right plants, at the right dose, plus the nutrients you've been running empty on.

Now here's the question I know you're asking. "What happens if I stop taking it? Will my supply crash again like it did every other time?" No, because this works differently. Think of it like clearing a blocked pipe instead of forcing water through it. Once the stress load eases, once the letdown starts firing on its own and your baby is nursing effectively again, your supply starts running on the natural supply-and-demand it was designed for. You're not chained to an artificial stimulation that quits the second you stop. You're getting the system back to doing the job itself.

That's exactly what Maravell was built to do. My name is Lauren. Six weeks ago I was the mom who did everything right.

Oatmeal every morning. Lactation cookies after every feed. Three kinds of tea. A water bottle I refilled so often it had a permanent spot on my nightstand. I pumped after every feed, then again at night, with alarms set for 2 AM.

And every week, the number on the bottle got smaller.

At the start I could pump 5 ounces. Then 4. Then 3. Then one night I sat on the kitchen floor with a bottle that had barely a layer at the bottom, while my baby, who had been drinking more and more, cried because she was still hungry.

More hunger. Less milk. And I had already given it everything.

If you have tried the cookies, the teas, the capsules and the pumping schedule, and your supply still keeps dropping, I was you. Exactly you.

Three weeks later it was 2 AM, the baby had finally fallen asleep, and I was crying on my kitchen floor. I had done everything right. Every single thing. And I was getting less than when I started.

At 2:47 AM I opened my laptop and typed: *why does my milk supply keep dropping even though I do everything right?*

Every site told me the same thing. Pump more. Drink more water. Eat more oats.

I had done all of it. Twice.

I kept digging anyway, because I couldn't go back to bed. Around 4 AM, I was scrolling through a mom group, still searching, and found something that changed how I saw the whole problem.

A mom had answered a post just like mine. She didn't say "drink more water."

She explained why the milk keeps dropping.

"Making milk isn't one job," she wrote. "It's three. Your body has to make the milk. It has to release it, so it actually comes out. And it needs enough left in the tank to keep doing both, day after night, night after day."

"Almost everything out there only works on the first job. Cookies, oats, teas, pumping more. They all tell your body: make more. But they don't help the milk come out, and they don't give your body back what pregnancy and birth took from it."

"So you do more of the same. And when it doesn't work, you do it harder. That's not you failing. That's one job getting all the effort, while the other two get nothing."

I read that three times.

I thought about every cookie I forced down. The tea I drank when I wasn't thirsty. The 2 AM alarms. Every time my supply dipped, I did more of the exact same thing, and every time I ended up emptier.

I wasn't doing it wrong. I had been working on one-third of the problem for six weeks.

"This is why I tell every mom the same thing," she wrote. "You don't need more effort. You need support for all three jobs."

Moringa and fennel, to support the signal that tells your body to make milk. Blessed thistle, to support the let-down, so the milk you make actually comes out. And vitamin D3, active B12 and amino acids, to refill what pregnancy and birth took from you, so your body has the energy to keep going.

And then the part that made me put my hand over my mouth.

"It's not just for you. The algae-based DHA and choline go through your milk straight to your baby. They help build her brain and eyes. So every feed gets better, not just bigger."
